```{r load}
source("R/metrics.R")
source("R/plotting.R")
r <- readRDS("results/cv.rds")
y <- r$y
oof <- r$oof
pct <- function(v, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * v)
f4 <- function(v) sprintf("%.4f", v)
```

The numbers on this page come from `scripts/run_cv.R`, which writes
`results/cv.rds`.

## Protocol

The clients are split once into a training set
(`r format(sum(!r$is_test), big.mark = ",")` clients) and a test set
(`r format(sum(r$is_test), big.mark = ",")`), stratified on the target. The test
set is not used on this page. The training set is divided into five stratified
folds, and every choice below (input set, model, hyperparameters) is made on
out-of-fold predictions: each client is scored by a model that did not see them.

Models are compared on the **log loss** of their predicted probabilities,

$$
\ell = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big[ y_i \log p_i + (1 - y_i) \log(1 - p_i) \big].
$$

Accuracy, recall and precision all depend on a decision threshold, and the
right threshold depends on what a default costs the bank, which is the subject
of part 4. The log loss is a proper scoring rule: it is minimised in
expectation by the true probabilities, so a model that wins on it is the one
whose probabilities can be trusted to set that threshold. The Brier score
$\frac1n \sum (p_i - y_i)^2$ is another proper score and is reported alongside.
The AUC only measures how well clients are ranked and says nothing about
whether a predicted 20% means 20%.

## Models

- **Constant**: the training default rate for everyone. Its log loss, the
  entropy of the target, is the reference every model has to beat.
- **Rule**: the single split `PAY_1 >= 2` (two months late in September),
  turned into a probability by using the default rate of each group. It is the
  first split a classification tree makes on this data, and a rule a credit
  officer could apply by hand.
- **Logistic regression** with an elastic net penalty. Continuous inputs are
  winsorised and expanded in natural cubic splines with four degrees of
  freedom, so the model is additive but not linear. The mixing weight
  $\alpha \in \{0, 0.5, 1\}$ and the penalty $\lambda$ are tuned.
- **Gradient boosting** (XGBoost) with learning rate 0.03. Thirty random
  configurations of depth, minimum child weight, row and column subsampling,
  L2 penalty and minimum split loss are tried, the number of trees being set
  by early stopping on the mean validation loss.

Each model is fitted on three input sets: the **raw** columns, the
**engineered** features of part 1, and both **combined**.

## Results

```{r table}
labels <- c(constant = "Constant", rule = "Rule PAY_1 >= 2",
            logit_raw = "Logistic, raw", logit_engineered = "Logistic, engineered",
            logit_combined = "Logistic, combined", xgb_raw = "XGBoost, raw",
            xgb_engineered = "XGBoost, engineered", xgb_combined = "XGBoost, combined")
ll0 <- log_loss(y, oof$constant)
tab <- t(sapply(oof[names(labels)], function(p) scores(y, p)))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = labels,
  `log loss` = f4(tab[, "log_loss"]),
  `pseudo R2` = sprintf("%.3f", 1 - tab[, "log_loss"] / ll0),
  Brier = f4(tab[, "brier"]),
  AUC = sprintf("%.3f", tab[, "auc"]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
```

The pseudo $R^2$ is McFadden's, $1 - \ell / \ell_0$, with $\ell_0$ the log loss
of the constant.

```{r plot, fig.height = 3.2}
n <- length(y)
L <- sapply(oof, function(p) -(y * log(p) + (1 - y) * log(1 - p)))
set.seed(1)
boot_idx <- replicate(1000, sample.int(n, replace = TRUE))
ci <- function(v) quantile(apply(boot_idx, 2, function(i) mean(v[i])), c(0.025, 0.975))
d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(labels)[-(1:2)], function(m) {
  q <- ci(L[, m])
  data.frame(model = ifelse(grepl("^logit", m), "Logistic regression", "XGBoost"),
             set = sub("^[a-z]+_", "", m), ll = mean(L[, m]), lo = q[1], hi = q[2])
}))
d$set <- factor(d$set, levels = c("raw", "engineered", "combined"))
rule_ll <- mean(L[, "rule"])
ggplot(d, aes(set, ll, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = rule_ll, linetype = "dashed", colour = palette_main["grey"]) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = rule_ll, label = "rule PAY_1 >= 2", vjust = 1.6, hjust = 1.05,
           size = 3, colour = "grey35") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4), size = 0.35) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(palette_main[c("accent", "dark")])) +
  labs(title = "Out-of-fold log loss by input set",
       subtitle = "Training set, five folds; bars are 95% bootstrap intervals over clients",
       x = NULL, y = "Log loss (lower is better)") +
  theme_report()
```

Differences between two models are measured on the same clients, so they are
much more precise than the intervals above suggest. The table gives the mean
difference in log loss and a 95% interval from a paired bootstrap over clients.

```{r diffs}
pair <- function(a, b) {
  dd <- L[, a] - L[, b]
  q <- quantile(apply(boot_idx, 2, function(i) mean(dd[i])), c(0.025, 0.975))
  c(mean(dd), q)
}
comp <- list(
  c("logit_engineered", "logit_raw"),
  c("logit_combined", "logit_engineered"),
  c("xgb_engineered", "xgb_raw"),
  c("xgb_combined", "xgb_engineered"),
  c("xgb_engineered", "logit_engineered"),
  c("logit_raw", "rule")
)
dt <- t(sapply(comp, function(cc) pair(cc[1], cc[2])))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  comparison = sapply(comp, function(cc) paste(labels[cc[1]], "vs", labels[cc[2]])),
  difference = sprintf("%+.4f", dt[, 1]),
  `95% interval` = sprintf("[%+.4f, %+.4f]", dt[, 2], dt[, 3]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrr")
dd <- setNames(as.data.frame(dt), c("m", "lo", "hi"))
```

**Feature engineering.** For the logistic regression the engineered features
are the largest gain on this page: the log loss drops by
`r sprintf("%.4f", -dd$m[1])`, two thirds of the gap between the logistic
regression and boosting on the raw columns. Boosting gains much less,
`r sprintf("%.4f", -dd$m[3])`, but the interval excludes zero. Trees presumably
find most of what the features encode by themselves, except the ratios and the
alignment of payments with statements, which they cannot build from single
splits. Adding the raw columns back helps the logistic regression a little more
and does not help boosting significantly.

**The rule is a hard benchmark.** The one-split rule reaches a pseudo $R^2$ of
`r sprintf("%.3f", 1 - tab["rule", "log_loss"] / ll0)`, against
`r sprintf("%.3f", 1 - tab["logit_raw", "log_loss"] / ll0)` for the logistic
regression on the raw columns, which is the model most analyses of this data
set report. A model has to earn its complexity against `PAY_1 >= 2`, not
against a constant.

**Choice of models.** Two models are carried forward:

- **XGBoost on the engineered features**, the main model. The combined set is
  not significantly better and has twice as many columns.
- **Logistic regression on the engineered features**, the interpretable
  reference. It is behind boosting by `r sprintf("%.4f", -dd$m[5])`; part 4
  checks whether that gap is worth anything once it is converted into money.

```{r hyper}
bx <- r$tuning$xgb_engineered$best
bl <- r$tuning$logit_engineered$best
```

The selected boosting configuration has depth `r bx$max_depth`, minimum child
weight `r bx$min_child_weight`, row and column subsampling `r bx$subsample` and
`r bx$colsample_bytree`, L2 penalty `r bx$lambda`, minimum split loss
`r bx$gamma` and `r bx$nrounds` trees. The logistic regression uses
$\alpha = `r bl$alpha`$ (lasso) and $\lambda = `r signif(bl$lambda, 2)`$.

## Caveats

- The hyperparameters were chosen on the same folds that produce these scores,
  so the scores are slightly optimistic, for the selected boosting model more
  than for the others since it was picked among thirty. The test set gives the
  unbiased figure in part 3.
- The bootstrap intervals resample clients but not training sets, so they
  ignore the variability that comes from refitting the models. Part 5 repeats
  the whole procedure over several splits.
